subsubtopic: PROPOSAL TO CLOSE RURAL POST OFFICES ON SATURDAYS- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the new postal regulations being brought into effect by the Canada Post Corporation will cause the closing of rural post offices across Canada on Saturdays. It is apparent that absolutely no thought was given to the rural and farming communities of Canada or their lifestyle, because they rely on the post offices being open on Saturday to conduct their business. Saturday is farmers' day in the small communities across our country as is evident by the resurgence of Saturday farmers' markets. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Kindersley-Lloydminster (Mr. McKnight):
That this House direct the minister responsible for the Post Office to direct Canada Post to provide service on Saturdays for rural Canadians according to their needs.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED URANIUM REFINERY AT BLIND RIVER, ONT.- MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has consistently rejected the requests of the concerned citizens of Algoma-Manitoulin to look into the safety of the proposed uranium trioxide refinery in Blind River, Ontario. The uranium refinery in Port Hope, Ontario, has been found releasing radioactive waste into the atmosphere exceeding permissible concentrations; AECL has acted irresponsibly in issuing licences and inadequately monitoring radioactive emissions at the Port Hope refinery, and AECL is now allowing another uranium refinery to be built at Blind River, Ontario. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Beaches (Mr. Young);
That the Minister of National Health and Welfare advise the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to discharge the AECL of its duties and responsibilities in the proposed Blind River refinery immediately, and that an independent team of inspectors be established with the mandate to enter the Port Hope refinery to undertake an independent base line health study and decide whether the Blind River refinery should proceed.

subsubtopic: INCREASED TAX EXEMPTION SOUGHT FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The minister will know that over 1.5 million working mothers in Canada who must pay child care expenses have been victimized once again by the minister's latest budget which has left unchanged the child care expense deduction. Child care costs have soared. The minister, by deindexing personal exemptions, will force these working mothers to bear a portion of the $1.3 billion extra tax to be generated by this measure.
I want to ask the minister again why this injustice was not changed despite repeated demands from this side of the House,
Oral Questions
despite representations by women's groups to the minister, and despite recommendations of the federal task force on domestic workers, which recommendations were released by the Department of Employment and Immigration in 1981. The task force said that child care expenses are as legitimate as other business expenses.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASED TAX EXEMPTION SOUGHT FOR CHILD CARE EXPENSES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I disagree with the hon. member when he states that the budget has victimized persons raising families. In fact the capping of the indexation on family allowances has been more than compensated. For families receiving the child tax credit there is an increase for this year of $50. The hon. member ought to know that the most needy families, 1 believe those with incomes of less than $30,000, have been more than fully protected as a result of the capping of indexation on family allowances.
The hon. member raises, of course, another question, namely, the over-all matter of how child care expenses are treated under the Income Tax Act. As I have had occasion to tell the House on previous occasions, the matter is the subject of a review by an interdepartmental committee under the leadership of the minister responsible for the status of women.

Madam Speaker, does the minister not realize that the $50 extra child tax credit is a small token when compared to the extra burden of the $1.3 billion tax increase which these women are going to have to pay and the extra tax that they are having to pay because of the child care expenses. These average about $4,000 a year while the minister allows them a deduction of only $1,000 per year per child. This is way in excess of the $50. According to the report of the National Welfare Council, 41.5 per cent of families headed by women were below the poverty line in 1980. These women desperately need the relief that this side of the House and these groups are requesting.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think it is important to keep separate the issues which the hon. member has raised in his two questions. The first issue that has to be examined is the impact of indexation of family allowances on recipients of the child tax credit, namely, those families most in need in the country. For those particular families whose family allowance indexation will be capped there will be a more than compensating payment in the child tax credit. As I recollect, the loss per annum per child is about $17, and again for this year the child tax credit is $50 per child. For those families the result of the budget is to make them better off. subsubtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CAPPING INDEXATION OF PENSIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. It involves about 120,000 retired public servants, 30,000 retired Armed Forces people, and 5,000 retired members of the RCMP. Given that former public servants who worked from 30 years to 50 years for the federal government contributed 6.5 per cent of their earnings for basic pensions plus one per cent for indexing in order to secure a full pension when they retired- this was not only a condition of their employment; it was confirmed by law in the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act-and given that the June budget has capped the indexing of these pensions at 6 per cent, under what authority is the government doing this? Why is the government breaking its promise to former employees who are in the sunset years of their lives, by cutting off part of their pensions when many of these people are barely making both ends meet now?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CAPPING INDEXATION OF PENSIONS

referred to the full pensions which are being received and will be received by retired public servants. Obviously there is no intention to affect the pension rights of retired public servants. What is intended is to cap the indexation at 6 per cent. Public servants will obviously receive increases in subsequent years, but the increases will be 6 per cent and 5 per cent. The impact, of course, of that capping of indexation can be minimized, and will undoubtedly be minimized as we make progress toward the 6 per cent target for inflation.
The hon. member should join us in the campaign to bring about a 6 per cent inflation rate because, in so doing, he will be coming to the aid of these retired public servants. The hon. member asked under what authority. Obviously that authority will be sought from Parliament by way of legislation in order to achieve the objectives of the government.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. It concerns both the consistency and the credibility of the government's so-called war on inflation. Yesterday in the House, the Prime Minister said, in response to a question, that no matter how high inflation goes, workers would be expected to hold their wage demands down to 6 per cent or, in his words, legislation would have to be considered.
Just a week ago the Minister of Finance said in the House, when dealing with the same question, that the question of comprehensive wage and price controls was not in the cards. Will the Prime Minister clarify this uncertainty? Are wage and price controls a possibility that will be inflicted upon the people of Canada this fall, or are they not?

Madam Speaker, I rise on a brief point of order arising out of the conduct of the proceedings under Standing Order 43.
You will recall that at the end of the 15-minute period normally allotted for motions under Standing Order 43, I attempted to raise a point of order. The Chair commented at that time that it was impossible to do so, undoubtedly thinking that the proper time was at the end of the question period.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that it was never the intention behind the rule changes to confine the raising of points of order and questions of privilege strictly to the end of the question period. Today's proceedings is evidence of how the strict application of that sense of the rules is very wrong.
It was my intention to raise the point of order and to suggest that the Chair seek the unanimous consent of the House not to see the clock and to put the question on the motion under
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
Standing Order 43 that was before the Chair. It does no good for me to raise the point of order at this time because we are 45 minutes beyond the event.
Probably all members on the government side, and certainly all members in the official opposition, would have liked to have seen that question put.
I would suggest, Madam Speaker, that in the future the Chair entertain points of order of that nature. It will be necessary for the Chair to hear a line or two at least in order to establish whether a valid point has been raised. Perhaps the Chair might take that into consideration in the event that similar occasions might arise in the future. I merely raise it for that purpose at the present time.

There are serious matters to be criticized, and I think Your Honour was absolutely correct in the procedure followed.

Madam Speaker, there is something I should like to clarify for the House. On June 17, 1982, and I am referring to page 18551 of Hansard, I gave an answer to a member of the New Democratic Party concerning Bill C-60 and said to him then that the bill would be proclaimed before the end of June. Before giving him that answer, I had consulted the minister sponsoring the bill, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who had told me that it was entirely possible and in fact had confirmed that the bill would be proclaimed before the end of June. After my answer of June 17 to the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources advised me that, owing to certain events, it would not be possible to proclaim that bill before the end of June.
Under the circumstances, with a view to setting the record straight and explaining the answer I gave to the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke, I should like to say to him that when I gave my answer 1 did so on the strength of the information provided to me by the minister responsible for the bill and that subsequently, owing to certain events, the minister told me that it could not be done. I would therefore urge the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources why the bill could not be proclaimed before the end of June. I wanted to put these remarks on the record so that in all fairness the hon. member be given an opportunity to ask for an explanation which the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is quite prepared to give.

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Lapointe (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased with this opportunity to take part in the debate on this very important budget brought down by our colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on June 28. My concern will, of course, be mainly with measures affecting small and mediumsized businesses in Canada. However, before I go any further, Mr. Speaker, I shall first take a few moments to outline what, I feel, should be the attitude of the various economic partners in Canada. Mr. Speaker, it is this attitude that is proving to be a prime factor in our struggle to get this country out of its present problematic situation.
Only last week, I had an opportunity to speak in Toronto at a conference on small- and medium-sized businesses organized by the Financial Times, and the theme of this special conference was: Private enterprise-How to make it survive and prosper. The theme was very apt, in view of the recession that is affecting industrialized countries the world over. Falling growth rates, rising prices and continuing unemployment, that is the general situation today, to a greater or lesser extent.
As the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech, the present recession is affecting both developed and developing countries, and the tragic part is that some of the causes of this recession are beyond our control. This was more or less the point that the Chairman of the Economic Council of Canada was trying to get across when he said two weeks ago that we should not expect Canada to get the world out of this recession on its own. A recession, Mr. Speaker, has a number of causes. Whoever is in government, in business or in the labour sector will be quick to blame one of the other sectors or economic partners and make them out to be the cause of all the ills besetting us today. Some people feel that the unions have made life too easy for workers, whose productivity has gone down while wage demands have become excessive. Another view is that businessmen and women should reduce their profit margins and thus slow down price increases. And it seems that
everyone, Mr. Speaker, feels that governments at all levels should reduce their spending. Granted all these statements have some truth to them, and there are things to be criticized in every group. But I also feel, Mr. Speaker, that this is part of the problem. So many of our economic partners in society today tend to look only to their own interests, and as a result, it is too often overlooked that any action taken by unions or business or government will inevitably have an impact on the other groups. Because of our isolationism, we cannot forget that society consists of a number of groups that are interrelated and that any action by one will have an impact on the others. A union trying to obtain wage increases for its members that are equal to or in excess of the inflation rate often forgets that in doing so, it is actually feeding inflation. On the other hand, businessmen or women who regularly decide to increase prices in order to compensate for failing incomes, are also giving inflation another nudge upwards. The fact is that we are just like the dog that is chasing its tail. Everyone knows he will never catch up with it.
To get out of our inflationary spiral and create a sound economic climate, we must make the necessary sacrifices now. Of course, in this network of relations between the main economic partners, governments are also part of the solution. They have often been described as organizations that try to please everyone and succeed in pleasing no one. There is some truth in this as well. All the members of this House and the members of the government have a duty to strike a sometimes very fragile balance between often conflicting demands by the various groups that constitute our society. This situation often leads to results that may or may not be very popular. For instance, establishing social programs or protective measures to help people cope with economic problems will be seen as socialism by some, while to others, granting tax rebates to business is tantamount to helping the rich become richer. In fact, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of politicians opposite who do very little to correct the latter impression. However, before we can break the inflationary spiral which is the principal cause of our economic problems, we shall, whatever our activity sector may be, have to look beyond our immediate surroundings and get out of our isolation. We must try to understand the needs and aspirations of others. And before getting together, we must get rid of our prejudices. It will not be easy, especially if demands are made in anger, whether through the media or in this House. Some major steps in this direction have been made during the last few months, for instance, by the Minister of Finance, who with some of his cabinet colleagues went on a Canadian tour of consultations with business and labour. I read in yesterday's Toronto Star that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance will be meeting the President of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. McDermott, some time on Friday, and Friday
July 7, 1982

afternoon, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister are having a special meeting with prominent businessmen.
Personally, since 1 became responsible for the portfolio for small businesses, I have tried to maintain frequent contacts with directors of small and medium-sized businesses in Canada, and 1 shall continue to do so. My point is that I shall continue to present to my cabinet colleagues the views of Canadian businessmen and women. Mr. Speaker, such contacts or discussions, as I said before, must be positive, because the task before us is overwhelming. This is what the Minister of Finance referred to in his budget speech, when he spoke of solidarity. Regular discussions between the major economic partners in Canada are therefore necessary, but we also need strong leadership. That is why, in his budget, the Minister of Finance asked parliamentarians to set an example to other Canadians. I therefore am fully supportive of the measure aimed at reducing salary increases of members, senators and ministers. As the House is aware, the measure consists of a rollback of the increases we obtained at the beginning of this year. Furthermore, all public servants, and there are more than 500,000 men and women in this category working for Crown corporations, the Armed Forces and the public service, will receive salary increases of not more than 6 and 5 per cent over the next two years. With my colleagues, I am convinced that the responsibility of the public service with respect to inflation is not any greater than that of other sectors in Canada. However, the rest of society must understand that legislated restraint at the federal level must be followed very soon by voluntary restraint in other sectors. As pointed out in the budget speech, the alternatives, namely, increased inflation and recession or more extensive controls, do not afford a very attractive prospect. Although the indexing factor for pensions and income tax will also be limited in 1983 and 1984, namely, to 6 per cent and 5 per cent, the government has given those least able to protect themselves the assurance that they will not be destitute. The child tax credit has been increased by $50 and will continue to be fully indexed to help families with modest incomes. Everyone receiving the guaranteed income supplement in addition to the old age security pension will get a supplement to the G1S payment offsetting fully the limitation on indexation of old age security payments. As the minister announced in his speech, veterans' pensions will continue to be fully indexed.
As the Minister responsible for small businesses, Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to support the forceful measures announced in the June 28 budget. Although some small businesses are experiencing problems, like most of my colleagues in this House I have been receiving a tremendous amount of mail from entrepreneurs who want to expand their businesses or set up new ones. The $400 million assistance program to reduce interest costs for small businesses undertaking new investment is a new program that is being added to the
The Budget-Mr. C. Lapointe
many existing programs that are helping small businesses in Canada.
Speaking about these other existing measures, Mr. Speaker,
I would like to urge my colleagues on the other side to agree to extend the application of the Small Businesses Loans Act, which expired on June 30, 1982, as proposed in a bill tabled two weeks ago, so that financial institutions, caisses populaires and credit unions can continue to guarantee loans to small businesses. Everyone supports this legislation, Mr. Speaker, starting with small businesses, financial institutions and all the members of this House. Members opposite tell me that they need two days of debate. I find it strange that they would jeopardize the interests of small businesses for the vainglory of being able to say that they had two days of debate in this House. I therefore hope that hon. members opposite will agree to extend the application of the Small Businesses Loans Act to give small businesses access to the capital which they so badly need.
However, to come back to the $400 million announced in the budget to help small businesses undertaking new investment, this means that, over a period of two years, small businesses eligible for the program will be able to reduce by 4 per cent their interest costs on certain investments made between June 29, 1982, and March 31, 1983. This 4 per cent reduction in interest rates will apply to loans of a minimum of $10,000 and a maximum of $500,000. Small-business men, fishermen and farmers who purchase goods subject to depreciation or who finance research and development projects will receive as an incentive grants totalling $200 million this year and $200 million next year. If we add this up quickly, Mr. Speaker, we see that $400 million in grants at an interest rate 4 per cent lower than current rates means that small businesses, fishermen and farmers in Canada will have access to loans totalling $5 billion. This means that there will be an opportunity for small-business men, fishermen and farmers to demonstrate their dynamism, as they have always done in the past, and to prove that they are truly the backbone or the basic fabric of the Canadian economy. I am convinced that entrepreneurs, Canadian businessmen and women will take advantage of this measure which will help them gain access to capital at reduced interest rates for investment purposes.
It should be noted that this program does not replace the Small Business Bonds Program announced in the budget of last November. Small businesses, fishermen and farmers in financial difficulty remain eligible for the bond program for refinancing purposes.
In response to the wishes of hundreds of small businesses, in its budget of June 28, the government has also postponed to January 1, 1983, the 12.5 per cent tax on small business dividends. The purpose of this measure was to encourage small businesses to reinvest funds which could otherwise have been paid out as dividends. As this tax has been further postponed I hope that small businesses will continue to reinvest these funds

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Mr. C. Lapointe
in view of the cash flow problem which they are facing because of high interest rates and the present recession.
In another area, Mr. Speaker, since 98 per cent of building companies in Canada are small businesses, the grants totalling $300 million for the purchasers of new houses and the firsttime buyers of existing houses should stimulate substantially the building industry. Contractors owning small businesses represent 52 per cent of the building activity in Canada. Those engaged in house or apartment building should therefore be responsible for creating a large part of the 118,000 new jobs resulting from these grants. The initial $30 million allocation to the home renovation plan will be increased to $60 million, adding new stimulus to the housing industry. These direct grants under the small business investment assitance programs and the housing programs will have a snowballing effect on a whole range of other small businesses, from the mobile canteens visiting the construction sites, from hardware stores like we all have in our areas to building materials firms, sawmills, furniture manufacturers, etc. Mr. Speaker, the new jobs and economic activity generated by these two initiatives will contribute significantly to economic recovery.
The government had a rather narrow margin for manoeuvre between reducing expenditures on the one hand and the need for stimulating the economy on the other. In my view, the areas that will benefit from this stimulus, namely small businesses, housing, farmers and fishermen, were the optimal target for such stimulative action.
Some years ago, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Dennis McDermott, the then president of the United Auto Workers was asked what was in his view the best way to stimulate the automobile industry. His answer was interesting. He answered at the time, and I quote:
Put the housing industry back to work, and my workers will get their jobs back.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is my view that the new housing program coming on top of all the programs announced in the November budget will not only help create 118,000 new jobs in the housing area, it will in turn give a shot in the arm to the automobile industry among many others.
Along with his June 28 budget, the Minister of Finance, tabled a discussion paper on possible investment measures, in order to stimulate discussion on how to ensure access to capital to small businesses. As indicated in the budget, a committee of prominent Canadian economists and tax experts has been given the responsibility for studying the feasability of various proposals. What is the purpose of the white paper tabled and the committee that started meeting on Monday, Mr. Speaker? It is to study measures intended to tax interest earned only to the extent where it exceeds the current inflation rate for Canadians investing funds in a new form of term deposit. Second, to tax capital gains on that part only that exceeds the inflation rate, in the case of Canadians purchasing common
shares of Canadian corporations. Third, to provide a 3 to 6 percentage point reduction on mortgage rates for new homes. Fourth, the possibility for small businesses, farmers and fishermen to secure loans for new capital investment at interest rates lower by 3 to 6 percentage points than prevailing rates.
The committee shall table its report by the end of September on the feasibility of those measures. It is important that the committee table the report soon, in order that the approved initiatives can be implemented as soon as possible.
It is also important to note, however, that the need for these initiatives and others to reduce government expenditures is dictated by inflation. Were it not for the specter of inflation, the confidence in our Canadian economy under normal conditions would be enough to encourage investments and job creation.
Such is the budget message. We must fight inflation together, while ensuring that jobs will be created and that no one among the less fortunate will suffer.
As 1 said, at the beginning of my remarks, I urge our economic partners to better co-operation. We cannot go on bickering from opposing positions. Prejudice and sour comments can do no more than hide the real problem. Mr. Speaker, we all belong to a country with a tremendous potential but going through difficult times. With our vast human, intellectual and physical resources, we can get out of this predicament.
I should like to conclude by quoting in part remarks which the Business Council on National Issues directed three weeks ago at my colleagues of the Cabinet:
This is clearly a time when productive discussion is most likely to flow from considering prospects for the future rather than recriminations related to the past. The occucpants of a lifeboat at sea are not likely to improve their chances of survival by arguing over how they got there. However, it is useful to know where lies the nearest shore.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is showing us this shore by setting up a recovery course of 6 per cent instead of maintaining a recession course of 12 per cent.
