subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think 1 understand why the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) is having such difficulty explaining the situation to the hon. member for Bramp-ton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid). Basically his understanding is that it is pointless to quarrel in a lifeboat about how one got there. Certainly some consensus on where the boat is going is the important part, but the minister missed the point, that is, that the lifeboat is absolutely full of holes at this point, and it is every man for himself. That is a true description of the state of affairs in Canada today. Of course, the lifeboat is the Government of Canada and its budget.
I approach this debate with some trepidation. I feel almost like a novice because this is the first opportunity I have had to speak in a budget debate on economic matters. I am almost a maiden in the lifeboat. I am confused. I have heard government members across the floor make some excellent, spellbinding speeches. I listened to an individual for whom I have tremendous respect, namely, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres), give a very learned and detailed speech. He gave percentages, facts and figures on complicated investment programs, but when I talk to people in my riding I realize that he might as well have been speaking Latin. In some instances our function as communicators fail.
The speech by the Minister of State for Small Businesses was excellent in terms of the detail and the concepts involved, as well as his explanations, but he might as well have been speaking Latin. His speech was excellent until the lifeboat analogy at the end. When we listen to government members we hear that they have identified the problems all by themselves, that they have developed the programs all by themselves and that they are better than sliced bread. But in reality that is not the perception of people outside the House. They are confused; they are wondering what is happening. I am confused.
I listened to the member of the official opposition from the province of Quebec when he made his speech last night. His speech was typical of those of many of the members of the official opposition. When he talked about the budget document I heard him say that it must have been put together by hypocrites, brigands and incompetents. 1 am confused because I
The Budget-Mr. Skelly
know many of the members opposite and they do not fall within that category. They are individuals who work very hard and are very conscientious. I know that individuals in the official opposition share the same sentiments about those members because they certainly are those kinds of people. Therefore, I am confused and I think that confusion extends to most people in the country.
We have been given many figures, which in most cases are quite accurate. Hon. members have talked about unemployment running at 11 per cent and inflation running at 11.5 per cent. They have talked about increasing bankruptcies of farmers, fishermen and small businesses, as well as the plight of home owners. They talked about the rising deficit and the incredible government spending. There is no point in repeating those facts and figures now because they are well known to the House and the people throughout Canada.
While we have gone into great detail in attempting to be technicians manipulating the finances of Canada, I suggest that we may have forgotten one small but important aspect of our function, and that is our job of being communicators. I believe that the people of Canada are completely confused about the budget. They do not understand the budget process or its purpose. I believe that Canadians are becoming even more confused when they sit down to try to rationalize the cost of running this place, which is somewhere between $100 million and $120 million a year. It must be very confusing for them to figure out a balanced cost-benefit analysis of the operation of this entire place. As communicators, I suggest that it is our job to attempt to clarify that confusion for Canadians. In fact, I am hard pressed, and certainly other members are hard pressed, to attempt to understand what we have done in a constructive manner for Canadians when we see this document put before us today.
1 have concluded that there are five steps to this budget process. While it certainly cannot be examined in a simplistic way since it is such a complex document with many supporting assumptions and facts, it might help me and hopefully some others to attempt to do that. I think the budget is mainly concerned with the identification and priorization of problems. In order to identify what those problems are, a consensus and co-operation are required at the outset.
It is interesting to note that we have profound disagreements with the government. It says that inflation is the major problem, while we have said that it is not the exclusive problem. We believe there are a combination of problems, such as high interest rates, unemployment and high inflation. As well, these are symptoms of much deeper problems, which the budget itself does not address and which the entire budget process has ignored. It is important to note, however, that there has been great confusion in the country and a loss of confidence in the government which, through the process of osmosis, has led to a great loss of confidence in the operation of this place. If our economic recovery begins with the identification and priorization of our problems and we cannot even agree on what those

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Skelly
problems are, how can we communicate to the people what our principal difficulties are?
Once these problems are identified by whoever is responsible for that, the next step is to develop programs which address those problems. Hopefully these programs will prove beneficial in the long run. While the government talks about sharing the burden and tightening our belts, surely these programs can only be developed with consensus and co-operation and a commitment to sacrifice and share. Unfortunately, there are widely varying points of view on this subject in the House.
It is interesting to note that these splits occur in different ways. The government sees high inflation rates as the problem and therefore takes a monetarist approach which involves the application of restrictive and repressive restraint programs as a cure. This approach, when reduced to its final form, will result in the strangulation of the economy in order to kill demand and expectations, which unfortunately lead into a recession when they occur in the prevailing circumstances in the country today. We do not agree that this is the main problem. However, it is interesting that it appears that this is the program which has been designed and preferred by the official opposition as well. Therefore, there is consensus, in spite of the inflammatory terms that have been used. The definition of the program and the identification of the problems by the Conservatives are the same as the government's, but I think the government has outflanked the official opposition to our right. This policy brought in higher interest rates than the Conservatives were willing to bring in and higher energy rates than the Conservatives were willing to bring in. It is surprising that the government has seemed to have outflanked the Conservatives on our right.
The next step in the budget process seems to be an analysis and explanation of the costs of those programs. People seem to be confused about this aspect as well. While the government attempts to fulfil its role as communicator, with the Minister of State for Finance speaking Latin last night and the Minister of State for Small Businesses speaking Latin today very effectively, it has not really communicated the essential message to Canadians. The government appears to want to spend about $78 billion this year in the execution of its programs. In order to spend this money it wants to create a $20 billion deficit. It is telling Canadians that its programs will not stop high unemployment, the bankruptcies of small businesses, farmers and fishermen, and it will not prevent home owners from losing their homes, nor will it reduce the deficit or improve the efficiency of its spending in Canada. It essentially wants to spend $78 billion and run up a $20 billion deficit in implementing programs in which the people do not have confidence. Canadians still anticipate that the economy will continue to sink. I have not heard one member of the government stand up and say that the economy will turn around and improve. This anxiety is a result of a failure of communication at the first level as well as a failure in the entire concept of presenting these facts.
The fourth step in the budget process involves an explanation of how revenues will be raised. Certainly these programs must be developed. The costs have to be assessed and then an
explanation given to the people of how these revenues will be raised. The government's explanation was fairly clear, I suggest. It was that these revenues have to be collected from non-tax sources and through taxation. The government listed a number of those sources.
The fifth step concerns the matter of taxation. This is one aspect of the budget in which individuals responsible for promoting this document must be scrupulous and work carefully to explain two particular reasons for taking money from the pockets of the taxpayers. One is that the money is needed and will be well spent, and the second is that the burden or liability for tax is spread fairly. However, this is not what the government has done. It has indicated more clearly than in any of the other steps in the process that the money will come out of the pockets of civil servants. This money which is to fight its anti-inflation program will come out of the pockets of senior citizens and people on fixed incomes and from a rather clever increase in the taxes of middle and lower-income Canadians. Ultimately this will reduce the spending power of that group of Canadians who might have been able to help reverse the trend which is occurring in some parts of Canada, had they received some modest stimulation.
So it strikes me that the budget process has five steps in it, and that it is very confusing for people. 1 think the government has missed the point in the whole exercise. When one observes how those five steps work, one finds that the government is telling people that it wants to spend $78 billion and incur a $20 billion deficit, mortgaging the future of Canadians on programs which no one really believes will resolve the problems that seriously affect Canadians.
The budget and the process through which the government has gone over the last few months is really communicating a message to people, and they are beginning to react and to respond. It is interesting to find that in a budget such as this, which attacks civil servants or the public service and which encourages the provinces to attack their civil servants, and which reduces already abysmally low pensions in this country by reducing the ability of the fund to keep up with the inflation rate, one is communicating one message. But certainly when the government turns around and, no strings attached, hands $2 billion to the oil companies which are being pressed, but not as pressed as the small businesses in the 16 communities in my riding which are going bankrupt, bang, the government is communicating its message, which is, "Goodbye and good luck." But when the oil companies begin to squawk, our old buddies like Imperial Oil and the others we have mentioned in the House, the government whips out the cheque book and writes a cheque for $2 billion, no questions asked, no strings attached. My colleague points out that under the petroleum incentives program they will be handed another $6 billion, but that will occur in time, of course. However, the government is communicating a message, and that message is being translated into an attitude and a reaction in the minds of people.

July 7, 1982

The Minister of State for Small Businesses developed the appropriate analogy. The people are getting the message that the government and the country are similar to a lifeboat full of holes, and maybe it is every man for himself. Look at Olds-Didsbury. Look at my riding. When the Western Canada Concept, which I guess is the equivalent of separatism in the west, arrived in my riding a year ago, it managed to draw six people to a meeting. But now there is such a turnout that it cannot hold meetings in the rooms which have been booked, and the meetings are held in shifts. There are signs throughout my constituency, "We have had enough". "Let's free the west", as the bumper sticker says. One should compare a lifeboat full of holes with writing a $2 billion cheque for the oil companies with no strings attached and then wishing the businesses, home owners, fishermen and forestry workers who are out of work, "Goodbye and good luck". These programs do nothing for forestry and nothing for fisheries. They are essentially left on their own. Even a recovery, because of poor economic planning, will not assist them.
The other matter is the bail-out of Dome. Again, we in this House are quite prepared to look at a set of companies which develop because of the lack of a competition policy. There is a lack of any sense of control involving the question of whether the development of these megacorporations would be in the interests of Canada, yet we develop them. They ran into enormous problems, but now the government whips out its cheque book and says, "We will help to bail you out", and the bank is behind them. That communicates the message, "Goodbye and good luck" to small businessmen, fishermen, farmers, those who are out of work, those who do not have any chance of employment. But when Dome comes to the door or the trough, when the banks come to the door or the trough, or when the oil companies come to the trough, they are paid off, bang. Maybe it is just poor communication and maybe I do not understand what the government is doing although, on the other hand, maybe I have a good idea. But my impression is that the government has really failed in its job as a communicator because I do not understand it, the people in my riding do not understand it, and the people of western Canada do not understand it. I bet that when we go to the polls the next time-and a change of government will not resolve this- the people will not understand it, and it will be, "Goodbye and good luck" to the present government.
So, where are we? In this sort of sad state of affairs there seem to be three problems. I would like to share my insight for whatever benefit it may be to the members of the House of Commons and the people I represent because, being confused, I can only try to develop some kind of empirical observations and try to interpret them. The government has forgotten the purpose of the government process. It is really an accountability process by which the people who represent Canadians stand up and say, "These are what we see as the problems, these are what we see as the programs that will solve our problems, and these are the costs and how you have to share them." It is not a small triumvirate sitting at the front desks on the other side of
The Budget-Mr. Skelly
the House with an all-seeing eye that perceives the problems in isolation, develops the programs in isolation and then randomly imposes the costs on Canadian society without consideration of fairness or equity. It is a shared process, or there is no support.
One of the main problems is that that organization, the government, has failed to understand what the budget is. It is an accountability process. We had better get back quickly to that fact.
Concerning accountability, remember that the people to whom we must communicate are hon. members of the House who directly represent the millions of people in this country. If that communication fails, then everything done will be a failure.
The second main problem is the process of consensus and cooperation. This is a very complex nation with different accessibility to benefits. Ultimately, what we have is a problem.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for Pembina (Mr. Elzinga) rises on a point of order.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member's comments, as important as they are. We on this side of the House find it despicable that hon. members opposite, in the government, cannot maintain a quorum in the House of Commons when we are discussing a budget that they supposedly feel is so important. We just want to put you on notice, my friends, that this budget will not be passed if you do not maintain a quorum.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The point I was making is that there are basically three main problems in this process. One is that the government has forgotten that a budget process is one of accountability, and that is vitally important. The second is that the programs developed and the costs shared must be determined by co-operation and consensus. Essentially, the government has destroyed the sense of community within this country because it is made up of a small group of people who make the decisions, which ultimately exclude everyone else. There is one federal government but ten provincial governments. The federal government is but one player, yet it conducts a budget exercise without inviting them to participate. There are municipalities in this country whose budgets are larger and whose effect is greater than those of some of the provinces. However, they are not brought into the process. Large businesses, and in fact small businesses, are certainly a factor, as well as organized labour and those who have no power, basically those people living on fixed incomes without organizations to represent them. If they are not part of this process of consensus and commitment, then we will all be in serious trouble and we will ultimately see the destruction of the sense of community in this country. We hear, for instance, from the province across the river which says, "Our objectives and ambitions are not being fulfilled and we would like to separate." We see the development of the Western Canada Concept, which now has firm roots in Alberta and Saskatchewan and is growing in Manitoba. Therefore, the destruction of

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Shelly
the sense of community in this country is a serious problem which lies in the way this budget and other programs in the House are constructed.
I would point out one other factor, namely, the operation of the Thirty-second Parliament, which has two basic characteristics. One is an incompetent government. When one steps outside this House, one finds no hesitation in saying that it is a fact that the government is incompetent. Many of the people who have prime control have been here too long and have lost their sense of commitment and their belief in the potential of this country. They have said, "We have tried it all before and we cannot do anything. We must weather the storm." But there are people behind that government, behind those front benches, who seem to have ideas but are being held back. Maybe as the change occurs, maybe as we remove the leader, maybe as we remove the Minister of Finance and Governor Bouey, the symbols of this repression, something new will come forward. But basically, the government is tired and incompetent. It is a tough bullet to bite, but the other characteristic is that the official opposition is unscrupulous in its operation. I am not referring to individuals, because I know that some are sincere and honest, but certainly at the leadership end of that organization there is a group of people who confine themselves on the floor of this House to screaming and yelling at the Speaker, essentially showing contempt for parliamentary democracy and the foundation of government in this country. That has happened too many times, my friends and colleagues. The ultimate result is that they are not here to fulfil a responsibility to provide constructive alternatives to what has been suggested. They are here basically to disrupt for the basest of political reasons, a grab for power. I suggest that this can be rectified. It is the basic policy of a small group of individuals and it is a function of leadership. When you attack people over there and destroy them personally rather than attack the government with alternatives and constructive criticisms, you are doing a tremendous disservice to the entire operation of democracy in Canada.
Basically the government has failed in its understanding of the budget process and the need for accountability. Basically they have failed to understand the need for consensus and cooperation in the entire process. Ultimately, they are incompetent, tired and in need of change within their own organization. Survival is what is at stake.
Unfortunately, the official opposition in providing a service to Canadians has been basically dishonest. They have attacked and eroded the strength of parliamentary democracy in Canada. They have failed in this intellectually honest process of providing constructive criticism by attacking personalities. It is much like the trick of the ancient Roman emperors who preferred to bait bears and shed blood to distract people. They do this rather than provide constructive alternatives and state the policies they would put in place if they were in government. Believe me, it is obvious and lacking in their operation in the House.
What is the answer? There are four short points. Parliamentary reform will not make the House work better. Good faith and a commitment to an effective operation will. If we combine those two, parliamentary reform to make the process more efficient and to allow for greater integrity and personal performance based on supporting this institution, we will find more confidence and understanding of what we are doing. The second is government policy. Basically we are not talking about high interest rates, high inflation and high rates of unemployment. We are talking about a real disease in this country, the lack of a long-term industrial strategy to develop this economy. I am talking about the long term, the long haul commitment, the kinds of things people in this country can identify with.
The government has studiously avoided that. Why? I do not understand. Many Canadian sask for an indication of where we are going in the long haul so that they can make the sacrifices and work together. They want to know at least where they are going. All that most of them know is that fishermen and many businesses are going down the drain, and the budget will not help. It has been stated before that if we are going to establish and strengthen the sense of community in this country, we cannot suddenly drop a bomb in this chamber like the bomb that was dropped the other day, and hope that anyone will support it. There has to be more effective cooperation and consensus in developing those documents.
I now come to my fourth point or resolution. Certainly there are many more. Others will put forward more constructive ones. My final point is that there have to be some symbols of good faith. The operations of this House since the beginning of the Thirty-second Parliament have created confusion and a lack of commitment in this country, especially in the economic sphere. I ask other members of the House what kinds of symbols of good faith and sincere interest do we really have? I suggest you cannot do what this budget purports to do without a mandate. 1 know that the government will never resign and call an election. The Conservatives know that. Everyone knows it. That is impossible. However, that should be done as a result of a mandate, not just an ad hoc, off-the-wall arrangement.
If they were to offer to people Bouey's head or the head of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), basically it would indicate a change. It would be a symbol of good faith. Maybe we should have a replacement. Somebody new from the back benches might help.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak in this debate on the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) last Monday evening, a budget which in my view responds to the economic circumstances of the country at this time.
This budget offers Canadians a way to put an end to the recession and to speed our progress toward recovery. In this effort, it calls on all Canadians to join in the solution and creates a climate where other governments, business, labour and individual Canadians will be able to work collectively
July 7, 1982

toward bringing inflation down, which in turn will bring recovery within the interdependent context of our international economic relationships.
The policy of this government in its June 28 budget, while maintaining the framework of current monetary and fiscal policy, is to intensify its efforts to lead Canada out of economic recession. The thrust of the Minister of Finance's budget is to restore confidence, confidence in the future where inflation is reduced.
To do this the budget has a four-part action plan: first, bring inflation down to at least 6 per cent through a nationwide collective effort; second, reduce the impact of high interest rates, especially for small businesses, farmers, fishermen and home owners; third, create over 300,000 jobs through direct government action and indirectly through improvement in the investment climate; and fourth, maintain the integrity of our social security system.
Our social security system is a comprehensive system and one of the best in the world. It provides for the cost of bringing up children, for complete medical and hospital services for everybody, for retired people and for elderly people with no or very little income.
How will the June 28 budget bring about this four-part action plan? It will do it by attacking inflation, attacking high interest rates, reallocating funds to create jobs, housing incentives and tax proposals. I would now like to deal in greater detail with each one of these.
The first goal is to attack inflation. The immediate objective for all Canadians must be to cut inflation nearly in half. We must move from a close to 12 per cent inflation to a 6 per cent recovery. There are many forces acting on the Canadian economy which are outside of Canada's control. The high interest policy in the United States is a good example. Another example is that Canada is a trading nation and partners with whom we deal are also suffering from the effects of the worldwide recession and, as a result, international markets for our products are weak.
However, there are areas which we can control and which are within our control. One is our inflation rate. If we are to be competitive on the world market once the recession is over, then our cost structure will have to be lowered or we will be priced out of the world market on which we depend to market our resources.
Therefore, the government wants to reduce our inflation rate to 6 per cent over the next two years. To do this the government is asking all Canadians to share in the effort. The indexing factor applied to personal exemptions and tax brackets for the 1983 taxation year will be 6 per cent, and in the 1984 taxation year it will be 5 per cent.
The pay raises in the public service, which includes the Armed Forces, the RCMP and Crown corporations, will be limited to 6 per cent next year and 5 per cent the year after. Salary increases made in January, 1982, for Members of Parliament, cabinet ministers and Senators will be affected immediately by being reduced to 6 per cent for the rest of the year and next year and 5 per cent the year after that. All regulating prices under federal jurisdiction will be monitored.
The Budget-Miss Campbell
This will affect such areas as public transportation, communications and foodstuffs.
Effective January 1, 1983, increases in indexed social payments will be limited to 6 per cent and in 1984 to 5 per cent. These limits will apply to old age pensions, family allowances and public service pensions. However, they will not apply to people who receive guaranteed income supplements, which will be double-indexed to account for the reduction in the old age security; nor will these provisions apply to veterans. Those families who receive a child tax credit will see an increase of $50 in 1983 when they file their 1982 child tax return. This increase of $50 will offset the reduced indexation of the family allowance which will start in January, 1983.
What does this mean for old age security and family allowance recipients? In July of 1982 persons receiving old age security received $235.17. They would have received in January, 1983, $251.73. However, with the 6 per cent indexation introduced in the budget, they will now receive $249.23 in January, 1983. Those receiving family allowances would have received next January 1, $29.87, but with the 6 per cent indexation they will receive $28.87. As can be seen, indexation will continue but is being reduced to 6 per cent in 1983 and to 5 per cent in 1984.
The federal government wants to show Canadians that the fight to reduce inflation is serious and that all areas which the government controls will be working to see that inflation is cut in half over the next two years.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government is offering the challenge to all sectors of Canadian life to help reduce inflation. My own premier has accepted this challenge, and I hope all Nova Scotians, both in the public and private sectors, will see that by reducing inflation to 6 per cent the over-all buying power of their money will be enhanced.
Without the central theme of the budget committing us to restraint, there is no doubt that we would be caught in the vicious spiral which the Minister of Finance spoke of in his budget speech, when he said that this vicious spiral means that inevitably incomes chase prices, which in turn chase incomes and, he added, no one wants to be the first to accept a lower increase in pay. The government has now moved to face this challenge head on, calling on all Canadians to help the nation achieve its goal of recovery by lowering our demands on the economy.
I would now like to deal with the attack on high interest rates, the reallocation of funds to create jobs and funds for housing incentives. The government will not add to the present deficit but rather will reallocate the funds which will result from the 6 per cent and 5 per cent indexation. Some of these funds will be directed immediately to provide relief from high interest rates for small-business men, farmers, fishermen and home owners. It will do this by making available grants of up to $3,000 to help home owners with mortgage renewals costing

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Miss Campbell
more than 30 per cent of their gross family income. It will give relief to small businesses-and this includes fishermen-now, immediately, by reducing their borrowing rate by 4 per cent. It will provide more assistance for Canadian farmers by reducing their interest rate by 4 per cent, through the Farm Credit Corporation.
With the reallocation of funds the government plans to create jobs. Along with lowering inflation and lessening the impact of interest rates, we must also find and create jobs for the many unemployed. The goal of the budget is to create over 300,000 jobs over the next two years. The budget provides an immediate $1.4 billion for direct jobcreation and other initiatives. A sum of $300 million will go to existing programs that stimulate job creation in the private sector. Another $200 million will be added to direct job creation. This will bring this fiscal year's direct job creation to $657 million. This is over and above the new national training program financed at a level of $1 billion to modernize Canada's training system and prepare workers for the jobs of tomorrow.
Another $400 million will go to the housing industry. Furthermore, $400 million will go toward reducing the interest costs by up to 4 percentage points for two years on borrowings by small businesses and fishermen-both incorporated and unincorporated-to finance new investment in research and development. The program here will apply to loans to small businesses by financial institutions which will qualify for the new assistance program. These loans must be used toward financing purchases after June 28, 1982, and before March 31, 1983, of new depreciable property to be used in an active business in Canada. This will include government guaranteed loans to small businesses under the existing Small Businesses Loans Act. The program will also finance the expenditure on scientific research after June 28, 1982, and before March 31, 1983. It is important to note that loans which would go toward the purchase of land, automobiles or property for lease, will not qualify. This interest relief program should benefit businessmen who must borrow to make new job-creating investments.
Another $100 million will go to the interest assistance program for farmers in distressed financial conditions who require a loan and associated interest rebate to survive over the short term. This program will be administered under the Farm Credit Corporation for the next two years. The loans will be made at the regular Farm Credit Corporation interest rate, but a rebate of 4 percentage points will be provided for the first two years of the loan. Over the longer term, the new proposal for the indexed term deposit certificate will be in place to provide assistance on high interest rates for businessmen, fishermen, farmers and home owners.
I want to turn now, Mr. Speaker, to the matter of housing incentives. To start the recovery of the housing construction industry, the government offers a dynamic five-point program. First, the Canadian home ownership stimulation plan will provide a $3,000 grant to all buyers of a new home and firsttime buyers of an existing home. The program is effective as of June 28, the night of the budget. Buyers must first make a
down payment of at least 10 per cent, over and above the $3,000 grant. An existing home is a unit that has already been occupied and must be purchased before December 31, 1982, in order to qualify for the $3,000 grant. A new unit is a home which has never been occupied, or it is one that must be started before December 31, 1982 and purchased before December 31, 1983. The program is limited to homes with a value of up to $100,000 for most areas of Canada and in all areas of Nova Scotia.
People who want to build their own homes are also eligible for the plan. The grant will be available to owner-builders when the interest adjustment date is set on the mortgage by the financing institution. The next plan had been in existence but has been changed. Under the budget, the Canada mortgage renewal plan allows home owners who have to spend more than 30 per cent of their gross family income as a result of renewing their mortgage to be eligible for a grant of up to $3,000 to help offset the higher interest rates on their mortgage renewal. This plan will be in operation until the end of 1983.
The third proposal provides increased funding for the Canada home renovation plan, which makes available a 30 per cent grant for home renovations on contract work of a minimum of $2,500 and up to $10,000. The $10,000 contract would qualify for the maximum grant $3,000. The 30 per cent grant applies to home owners whose gross family income is $30,000 or less; above $30,000 there is a decreasing grant available up to gross family income of $48,000. This program will be in existence until the funds of $60 million are exhausted, and it has been very well received in South West Nova and elsewhere in Nova Scotia.
The fourth incentive to the housing industry is the non-profit and co-operative housing 1982 allocation which has been increased by 2,500 units. This will be of interest to many areas in Nova Scotia where people have built new homes under the co-operative housing program of CMHC.
Finally, the federal government's commitment to available rental housing was reaffirmed under the Canada rental supply plan for new rental units in a tight market.
The tax proposals contained in the budget are also interesting, and all Canadians will be able to take advantage of them. The Minister of Finance has set up a committee of prominent Canadian businessmen, accountants and economists to advise on the new tax proposals in the budget. The committee has already met with the Minister of Finance and will meet again. Their recommendations on the implementation of the investment initiatives should be forthcoming over the next few weeks.
The two new proposals of the budget are, first, the creation of the new indexed term deposit that would pay the investor tax-free interest on that part of the interest earned that reflects inflation. Funds accumulated in this way would be directed by the financial institution to purchasers of new homes and to
July 7, 1982

small businesses, farmers and fishermen investing in new plant and equipment at interest rates from 3 per cent to 6 per cent lower than market.
The second proposal is for a new registered shareholder investment plan where the investor puts his money in a fund that buys publicly-traded common shares in Canadian companies. The capital gains on the shares would be taxable at half rate as before, but only to the extent that they exceed the inflation rate.
Mr. Speaker, I have tried to speak on the many areas of the budget which are of interest to my constituents as well as other Nova Scotians and Canadians. The member who spoke ahead of me talked about communications. I challenge members opposite to read the budget papers. They will be effective if all Canadians are to fight the present recession and high inflation rates.
The economic situation facing the country is serious. Most of the industrial world shares the twin burdens of high unemployment and high inflation. There are no quick fixes, no easy solutions, but the budget now before the House offers a combination of proposals and a course that will, I am sure, lead to recovery. It is in this spirit that the Minister of Finance called on Canadians for their collective effort in overcoming our difficulties. I am confident that we can overcome these difficulties and return to better times.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) has admonished the whole country and asked us to read the budget. I must tell her that one of the problems the country has is that people have read the budget and that they have been affected by the last two budgets brought in by the same Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), so they are not really willing to take him at his word or take the Liberal Party at its word any longer.
When the Minister of Finance announced on June 22 that he would introduce a new budget to the House the following Monday, we in the opposition had some reason to believe that, after weeks and months of argument and debate and our telling the minister about the paucity of his economic programs, all this was finally beginning to have an impact.
The almost daily deterioration of all the economic indicators in this country, triggered by the minister's first budget and greviously aggravated by his second budget-that downward slide had at last, so we thought, brought this hear no evil, see no evil government to its senses.
Statistics have been used again and again in this chamber and across the country-statistics on unemployment, bankruptcies, foreclosures. We thought they had become so horrifying that not even this remote and autocratic government could ignore them any longer. Finally, the minister indicated on June 22 that there was to be a change. Finally there was to be a response to the calamity taking place in the country. Finally there was to be a new budget, tinkering here and changes there-call it what you will but at least there was to be some action.
On June 28, budget night, we got that action. This time the Minister of Finance surpassed himself. Given a third chance at
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
budget-making-although why he should have merited a third chance after all the damage he has done to the country only the Liberal caucus knows-he again managed to swing and miss. Not for him a comprehensive plan to relieve high mortgage rates and thus provide a widespread and permanent boost to our housing industry. Instead, he offers a one-time freebie that will do nothing to alleviate the 20 per cent mortgages that have to be paid year after year. Then he includes a vague proposal to reduce mortgage rates that will be examined and studied until late this year, even thought 70 per cent of all mortgages up for renewal this year will become due between June and October, in other words, before that committee has a chance to report and have its recommendations implemented.
Not for the Minister of Finance measures that would stimulate the private sector or increase productivity or tackle head on the appalling cost to this country of 1.5 million Canadians who are unemployed. That cost will be reduced only as job opportunities open up.
Instead, in the face of an additional $2 billion pay-out from the unemployment insurance fund since last November, the minister increases direct job creation by a measly SI00 million this year. With 1.5 million unemployed, that measly $100 million will produce jobs for perhaps 30,000 Canadians. What about the other million-plus Canadians who are unemployed? What all about all of those others who are going to be facing lay-offs between now and the end of the year? Oh, yes, he did promise to create jobs through something he calls "levered investment incentives". I wish he would explain to the business people of my riding what he means by levered investment incentives. Better still, would he just spell it out in plain English?
There was a time, it would seem, a time like this, that the minister would be called upon to take bold measures. Instead, what he does is raise his head up out of his bunker, survey the state of disaster all around him, and then duck down again. He ignores the crippling damage of high interest rates. He ignores the fact that government spending will increase 20 per cent this year over last year-no restraint on government spending. He ignores his own miscalculation of the deficit; it has gone from $10 billion to $20 billion in a period of seven months. Obviously simple mathematics is not one of the strong points of the Minister of Finance. He ignores all these calamities as he prepares to hunker down again. Instead, he selects and sends out the front line troops to Fight off the onslaught that his previous budgets have triggered. Who are they? Well, he shields himself behind the elderly, the unemployed, and the people with lower and middle incomes. In one last vain attempt the minister tries to shield himself and his government from the havoc that he and his colleagues have created year after year as they piled up deficit after deficit. It is not working, Mr. Speaker, and it is not going to work because the people of Canada have had to pay for the government's mistakes and the

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
mistakes of the Liberal Party for just too long. They have had to pay in terms of lost jobs, lost homes, high interest rates, spiralling fuel costs and, ultimately, in lost hopes, shattered dreams, insecurity and anxiety, and they are just unable to take any more.
What the people of Canada have to say to this government, Mr. Speaker, simply and clearly is this: we do not believe you. We do not believe the deficit is all due to the deterioration of the economy. We do not believe that $20 billion is all for unemployment insurance claims. We do not believe that every man, woman and child in Canada has cost this government $1,000 more than they have contributed in tax upon tax upon tax. They are saying: we do not believe our economic nightmare is the fault of American interest rates or Arab oil. They are saying: we believe it is the fault of an arrogant bunch of callous, cynical and cold-hearted incompetents who should not be trusted to run a parish bingo, let alone the finances of one of the most richly endowed countries in the world.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If there is one single thing that Canadians from coast to coast can agree upon, it is their lack of confidence in this government. This above all is the problem in Canada. The present budget has done nothing to alleviate the situation. However, Mr. Speaker, I honestly believe that no matter what this government would do at this point, it simply would not work because they have eroded the faith of ordinary Canadians. They have destroyed the trust that must exist between the government and the people. They have spent their substance in riotous living and now they are asking ordinary Canadians to pay for it. Is it any wonder that Canadians have become cynical, disheartened and frustrated?
Meanwhile, the government casts around looking for a solution to its problems. When will the Liberals realize that they cannot provide the solution because they are the problem? They are the problem because of the deception that they practise on the Canadian people. They are the problem because they fail to keep their word and because they say one thing and do another. How often have we heard from the Liberal Party the words "the just society", or "social justice and equity"? How often have we heard those words being mouthed? The November budget laid great emphasis on that word "equity". What a hollow mockery this present budget makes of the concepts of equity, fairness and compassion! Nowhere, sir, is this more blatant than in the harsh measures the government is taking to partially deindex personal income tax and partially deindex old age pensions and family allowances.
I would like to direct the attention of hon. members, Mr. Speaker, to that question of deindexation for a few minutes. Ten years ago the former leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, the hon. Robert Stanfield, began advancing a long overdue change in government policy. He said that people should not be bumped into higher personal income tax brackets unless their real incomes increased. He said it was wrong to have a tax system which took a larger and larger share of
people's incomes as inflation rose, without governments ever having to come back to Parliament to openly raise taxes. He said this was a deceitful way of going about increasing the government's revenue. He said that such a system not only defrauded the taxpayer but made government irresponsible and less accountable to the people's representatives.
When Mr. Stanfield first put that idea forward, it was spurned by the government of the day. During the 1972 election the then minister of finance, John Turner, argued that such a system would cost the treasury too much money, it was unnecessary because he said inflation was just a temporary problem, and the Americans did not do it so why should we? Then in October of 1972 the government lost its majority, barely holding on to a plurality in the House of Commons. Mr. Turner decided that a flip-flop might be in order and on February 19, 1973, he brought in a budget which pledged to index personal income tax brackets and exemptions fully to the rate of inflation beginning in the 1974 tax year.
Nor was this to be a short-term experiment. Speaking for the government, a government led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and including the present Minister of Finance and the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), Mr. Turner described his policy as "a lasting solution to this problem should inflation continue". He noted that a worker whose wages had risen only enough to maintain purchasing power in the face of rising inflation could be worse off under the then existing tax system because his higher nominal income would push him into a higher tax bracket. The government's stated intention, according to Mr. Turner, was to eliminate that unfair and unintended result from our tax system. Mr. Turner bragged that through his policy Canada was joining a very select group of countries which have eliminated the hidden revenues accruing to governments through the effect of inflation on a progressive tax system. His words leave no doubt that the policy shift was to be a permanent one in his words "a lasting solution should inflation continue".
In light of what happened on June 28, there is an echo of the poetic worthless pledge of some of the treaties with the native peoples where we find these words: "As long as the grass grows and the rivers flow." Because, Mr. Speaker, lasting solutions in the Liberal dictionary turn out to last nine years. So fundamental and so permanent did Mr. Turner consider this policy that he described it as "a major innovation in tax philosophy and practice" which though not complex would "take some time for people and governments to adjust to". Consequently, he concluded that it should come into effect only the following year.
When Mr. Turner brought in this measure back in 1973, inflation was 5.8 per cent. That is when he decided that the Liberal government should index the tax system up to 6 per cent. The step was so momentous that it was going to take a year for the country to adjust to it. Now with inflation at the rate of 11.8 per cent, double what it was in 1973, the Liberal
July 7, 1982

government is taking the first opportunity to deindex it to 6 per cent.
What will be the result of this reversal of policy of the Liberal government? People not now paying taxes will join the tax rolls even though they have had no real increase in income, and people now paying taxes will pay more. The real hyprocri-sy of the government's position is revealed in the government's own tables in its Budget Papers. These are found on pages 13 and 29. There the government projects that it will take in SI.3 billion between January 1, 1983 and March 31, 1984 as a result of this deindexing of personal income tax. In the process, the government will increase the tax burden on every group of taxpayers, except married couples with children earning less than $12,000 a year. Let me repeat that. The tax burden will be increased for every group of taxpayers except one.
Such a projected revenue increase of $1.3 billion is an admission by this government that it does not expect the program announced in the budget to reduce inflation to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent levels for 1983 and 1984. If it did, there would be no revenue gain for the government from partial deindexation. Yet the government said it is going to make $1.3 billion on the move. The government itself does not believe that it is going to be able to wrestle inflation down to 6 per cent. Otherwise, the government would not have put forward those revenue projections.
Similarly, an expenditure reduction of $260 million is forecast between January 1, 1983 and March 31, 1984 because of the partial deindexation of the family allowance and old age security pensions. Again, this assumes inflation will rise faster than 6 per cent in 1983 and faster than 5 per cent in 1984. In effect, the government is asking the beneficiaries of these programs, the beneficiaries of old age pensions and family allowances, to take significant cuts in both 1983 and 1984.
True, a few low-income families-with children receiving the child tax credit will come out ahead initially because the enriched tax credit more than offsets the reduction in family allowance due to partial deindexing. But by the end of 1984, according to the program, almost all families will lose because of the cumulative impact of partial deindexing for the 1983 and 1984 tax years. That is something the Minister of National Health and Welfare does not talk about. She does not mention the cumulative effect of deindexation.
Old age pensioners fare even worse. True, the poorest of them, those who qualify for the guaranteed income supplement and the spouses' allowance, do not gain; they merely do not lose under the new arrangements. But those who do not qualify for the guaranteed income supplement-the more than one million pensioners in this country, and here we are talking about many single people with total incomes starting at less than $8,500 a year and couples with total incomes starting at less than $14,500-will lose $80 in 1983-1984 and an additional sum of money in 1984-1985. That is what will happen to them.
The income of these people was indexed to inflation in the first place according to the policies of the Liberal government, copied and borrowed from Mr. Stanfield. But we gladly gave it to them because it was recognized that the elderly have no
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
levers to bargain effectively for higher incomes to offset the ravages of inflation. They do not have the levers other groups in society have. Thus it was felt that the purchasing power of their incomes should be protected. That protection, and the principle of equity it embodied, is now to be eroded for at least two years; or should I say, until the Liberal government meets its long overdue accountng with the voters of this country.
The erosion of equity this government is smugly presiding over hits you again, Mr. Speaker, when you examine the partial deindexation of the personal income tax on various income groups. Let me give the analysis of one economic consultant. Patrick Grady of Ottawa, in making his calculations, assumed an indexation factor of 11.7 per cent for the 1983 tax year and 9 per cent for the 1984 tax year. His findings show that the single taxpayer's partial deindexation will raise the effective tax rate for those earning $7,500 by 1.5 per cent in 1983, while those earning $100,000 will see their tax rate rise by only 0.9 per cent.
Now, that is equity? Where is the equity in this? A 1.5 per cent tax increase for those at the lower end of the salary scale but a less than 1 per cent tax increase for those who are well off, those in the $100,000 bracket. How can any member opposite justify that? Have they no conscience at all? Particularly, how can members opposite justify that after the budget of last November when the government cut tax rates for those earning $30,000 or more per year, with the biggest cuts coming for those making $50,000 a year? The social reformers in the Liberal Party, if there are any left-and I am looking at my friend, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey)- should hang their heads in shame at meekly accepting such regressive measures. Yet I would say that far from wearing sackcloth and ashes this government has the audacity, in the same budget in which it is socking it to the working poor, to publish a paper entitled "Inflation and the Taxation of Personal Investment Income", in which we find this statement:
The current indexing system has protected Canadians from large tax increases ... It operates well for income from wages and salaries, pensions, social security receipts and other transfer payments.
That is what the government says about the current indexing system. But then it goes on to gut that system for the next two years. How inconsistent, how inequitable, can a government be within the confines of a single budget? The government seems determined to plumb the depths of both those qualities-inconsistency and inequity. At the same time it becomes the profiteer, the chief beneficiary from deindexing the tax system. It is the one agency which makes money out of inflation. It is in the government's interest to keep inflation high.
The Minister of Pinance who once prided himself on his social conscience now seeks to rectify his mistakes, to correct his past blunders by going after the pensioner whose income is $700 per month. He is the new Ebenezer Scrooge but he now has an accomplice-the Minister of National Health and Welfare. She has not only rejected universality and equity by
19108

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Miss MacDonald
allowing the Minister of Finance to deindex those pensioners receiving only old age security, but she has casually turned her back as if she had no responsibility for them whatsoever. She said on budget night: "I can live with it and they, the pensioners, can live with it too." That is a very callous remark coming from anyone, but particularly from someone who does not have to live on $8,000, $9,000 or $10,000 per year.
She may indeed have battled for the cause of pensioners in cabinet. I would hope and trust that she did, but she lost out. She is losing out in another battle as well. Indeed, I am afraid that she is losing out in the major war which must be waged in the name of pension reform.
What has happened to the much publicized pension reform which the minister has been enthusiastically promising us for over a year now? She promised it last summer, she promised it last fall, she promised it this spring, she promised it this summer. Now, once again she has said that this much-trumpeted green paper on pension reform has been postponed until next fall. By the time we see the paper, I fear it will no longer be green but grey from old age, from being postponed for so very long.
What is clear is that pension reform is no longer, if indeed it ever was, a priority of the government. Poor people who are living below the poverty line are no longer a priority of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Why is it that essential social programs always have to be the first to be cut? The minister's promises of the past year now seem very hollow indeed. She accepts a cutback of $100 million in payments to pensioners as a result of the budget.
Instead, she could have argued for a cut of $100 million from the $670 million spent on the rental of premises by the government in the national capital region. It could have been cut if renting were carried out at the cost of average rental space throughout the national capital region. But it did not come from cutbacks in government rental. She could have argued for a reduction of $100 million in the amount spent on professional and consultants' fees which comes to more than $1 billion in the budget this year. That amount could have been cut back by $100 million. She could have asked that $100 million be taken from the $1.6 billion spent on the personal costs of ministers, such as motor car allowances and other personal expenses. That $100 million could have come out of that $1.6 billion. She could have argued that the $250 million spent on information and advertising by government be reduced to provide additional revenue. She could have argued for a reduction in the $2.2 billion spent on utilities, materials and supplies this year. She could have argued for a reduction in any of those areas but obviously she did not, so pensioners have to bear the brunt of a $100 million cutback as a result of the budget.
I said at the outset that there is a deep and fundamental loss of confidence all across Canada in the government. It comes about as a result of measures such as the ones about which I have been talking. There is no sector of our economy, no group of our people, no region of our country which is not affected by
that loss of confidence. This House may divide as it did last night 144 to 130 on the question of confidence, but make no mistake, Mr. Speaker, the country, our Canada, does not divide that way. The country is united in its rejection of any confidence in the government. I dare hon. members on the government benches, the Prime Minister, his cabinet and all Liberal backbenchers to have the courage to go to the country to find out what the people think.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in fact- and I am reacting to the words spoken by my colleague-after June 28, or to be more specific, after the House adjourned on June 30,1 did go to my riding and I certainly was not afraid to ask what people were saying about the budget. Naturally, many people who listened to the budget speech by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on Monday, June 28, were wondering which measures applied to which economic sectors and which individuals, and many of my constituents in Lotbiniere made the following comment, more or less: the budget seems to have some very good provisions, and according to the minister's speech, it seems we have the mechanisms to deal with the present situation, with inflation and with the recession, and that Canadians are being given the means to face up to the situation through the various programs announced in the June budget.
When I hear members of the opposition talk about the status of the Canada Pension Plan and family allowances and the problems in these two areas that come under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Health and Welfare- when I hear them say, for the sake of making political capital, that the people receiving these payments will be penalized and will have problems and that they are the ones who are going to suffer real hardship as a result of the June budget-Mr. Speaker, when I hear them speak this way, I have to protest, and I want to tell these people on the other side of the House that they are just indulging in petty politicking and trying to make the public and senior citizens believe they are going to suffer as a result of the budget. As far as the old age pension is concerned, the base payment is $239.73 in July, in October it will be indexed, and on January 1, 1983, it will be $249.23, as a result of the 6 per cent ceiling, otherwise it would be $251.73. However, these payments will continue to be indexed every three months. About 47 per cent of 2,368,569 Canadian pensioners are receiving the base pension. If they have the base pension, Mr. Speaker, this means they have other sources of income to live on, they have other income to make ends meet, and that income could be $15,000, $25,000 or $30,000. But whatever the pension system, old age security is a universal system and whether you have an income of $30,000 or $40,000, you get the base pension.
I think Canadians are aware of this situation, namely, that payments will continue as before until January 1, and then
July 7, 1982

they will be $2 less, but what is really important to Canadians is that nothing has changed for the remaining 53 per cent who are receiving the entire GIS or part of the supplement. In fact, the slightly lower indexation of the base pension will be entirely compensated for by double indexation of the GIS every three months, starting January 1, 1983. As far as the GIS is concerned, 1 think senior citizens in this country should know that a person who receives the guaranteed income supplement does not have sufficient income, statistically speaking, to live on the base pension alone. In fact, it means that the individual has no further sources of income. On the other hand, people receiving the base pension only have other sources of income which enable them to cope.
I would like to explain to Canadians and to the people in the riding of Lotbiniere what the situation is regarding double indexation, and what happens to those who will only receive the base pension. Double indexation will be applied to the GIS every three months, starting January 1, 1983. The July 1982 GIS payment will be as announced a few days ago, that is, a maximum of $240.67 for a single person and $185.55 for each spouse. Next January, these figures would normally be $252.61 for a single person and $194.75 for each spouse, but with double indexation, the cheque will be $255.11 for a single person and $197 for each spouse. In fact, people receiving GIS payments will be receiving more according to the measures in the June 28 budget. In any event, 1 think that trying to make political points on a subject like this is in very poor political taste. Earlier in the House, there were references to the status of people receiving the base pension only, and in fact, over 1983, people receiving the base pension will be receiving $55 less, and indexation will be 6 per cent instead of 11 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, as far as the base pension is concerned and the $55 per pensioner that the 6 per cent ceiling has made available for other uses, does the House think that these pensioners would not be happy to see that money spent on community development programs that will help people work and help the children and grandchildren of these senior citizens to find work? I am referring to senior citizens who are receiving only the base pension and who have other sources of income. I am sure they would have no objection, because I met senior citizens who are receiving only the base pension and considering the other sources of income they have, I think the $55 in question would be very usefully spent on job creation. I must protest most energetically against the insinuation that we are trying to make political points with senior citizens, and I can assure our senior citizens that job creation is very important for young people who are having trouble finding work. This money will be spent on putting them to work. That is the real situation, Mr. Speaker, and the important thing to remember in connection with what 1 said earlier is that starting January 1, 1983, GIS payments will be increased. People receiving GIS will be better off than they were before the budget. So there is
The Budget-Mr. Dubois
no reason to act like alarmists and indulge in petty politicking on the subject of senior citizens. And now, how does the budget affect family allowances? At the present time, family allowance, which is now $26.91 per child unless there is a different rate in Quebec and Alberta would normally go up to $29.87 by next January, but with the 6 per cent ceiling, it will only go up to $28.52, $1 and a few cents. Over 1982, the total allowance for one child will therefore be $322.92. In 1983, this figure would normally be $358.44 but will now be $342.24.
The rate of indexation will be 5 per cent in 1984. However, what is important with regard to family allowances is that of the 3,636,851 mothers who receive the allowance in Canada,
2.5	million are also entitled to the child care tax credit. These women will not be affected by the budget. The important thing to tell the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker, is that if the spouse's income is less than a certain amount-I believe it is now something over $20,000-the child care tax credit can be claimed. Those who need it most will therefore benefit from the budget of June 28, 1982.
In this regard, I want to point out that the child care tax credit, which amounted to $261 non-taxable per child this year and should have gone up to $293 in 1982, will be increased by another $50 as compensation and will therefore amount to $343 non-taxable per child in 1983. This will compensate for the capping of family allowances for the next two years. Once again, this is what happens in the case of a universal allowance system. Does the person with children and a family income of $50,000 or $40,000 a year need the child care tax credit more than someone with an income of $20,000 or less? That is why, as concerns the child care tax credit, deductions are made from a taxpayer's income, since those who are more hard-pressed need more money. This is what the budget of June 28 does. It provides $50 more and increases the amount from $293 to $343. Therefore, all Canadian mothers who are entitled to the child care tax credit because their spouse's or their own income is less than a designated amount will receive $50 more. These are the facts Mr. Speaker. This is not the proper time to play politics concerning family allowances and the pension system in Canada. This is important since, out of 3,636,851 mothers,
2.5	million are entitled to the child care tax credit, and they are the ones who will benefit and receive $50 more. This is the important thing to tell the Canadian people instead of trying to indulge in petty politics about this issue. That is why I wanted to begin my intervention by speaking about these two issues, the old age security pension and family allowances.
Mr. Speaker, other programs announced in our budget were received enthusiastically, at least in my own constituency. These programs deal with housing and concern the renovation of Canadian homes. This program will benefit construction workers, contractors, of course, and also realtors. Since June

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Dubois
28, many realtors in the major city of my constituency, Vic-toriaville, have telephoned me about this $3,000 grant to find out how it would be paid, and 1 must say that they were very happy to learn the facts. How many homes have been built by contractors who unfortunately cannot find a buyer? A great many! And how many contractors who could have started building new homes are not doing so because of the mortgage payments potential buyers would have to pay? The program which was announced on June 28 in the budget will benefit these people, Mr. Speaker. What I am trying to do is to explain these programs so that the Canadian people will know what we have done following the representations made by realtors, builders and representatives of the housing industry to help this sector, because it is often said that if the building industry is running smoothly, the wheels turn by themselves. The $3,000 grant will apply to the purchase of new homes, whether condominiums, duplexes, triplexes, row housing or single family units. The important thing is that a prospective buyer may opt for either a new home or an existing home. And if a person has never owned a home and wishes to buy an existing home and if that person is a first-time purchaser, he will be eligible for the $3,000 grant. There are, of course, certain conditions to be met.
So, two possibilities are covered. The situation where we have a new home on which construction has started by a certain date, a new home that has already been built but has never been lived in and, what is important to many couples, homes that are several years old. This is an opportunity for people, including young couples or even older couples who have never owned a home, to pay less for an existing home which may be 10, 12, 15, 25 or 30 years old and qualify for the $3,000 grant.
There is, of course, the 10 per cent down payment which must be considered, but even so, $3,000 is still quite substantial, considering the present interest rates. 1 also think that, to people who are trying to cope with the present situation in the construction industry, this program will be very important, especially those who were laid off for several months last year, because obviously, contractors-and quite a few have already called my riding office-are aware of the situation and are going to start building houses, and even with the present uncertainty regarding interest rates, a person who qualifies for the $3,000 grant has at least that, and in my view and not only in mine, Mr. Speaker, but also according to many of the people in my riding, it is a real incentive for this sector to get back on its feet.
What about other programs that already exists and that were well received when they were announced and even more so when we decided to allocate additional funds 1 am thinking of the Canadian home renovation plan. One of the existing programs is the RRAP for rural areas. To qualify for the
program, a municipality had to have a certain number of inhabitants, and many Canadians had been asking their members for programs for municipalities that did not have the requisite population for the RRAP.
That is why the Canadian government introduced the Canadian home renovation plan under which people would receive up to a certain percentage, namely, 30 per cent, which in many cases could amount to $3,000. Many contractors and people involved in home improvement were very pleased with this program to which $30 million was allocated. On June 28,
1982,	the Minister of Finance added another $30 million, thus enabling people whether they lived in a municipality, whatever the population-except for the RRAP program in rural areas-whether they lived in a municipality, a town of 50,000, 100,000 or 200,000 inhabitants, and provided they met the income requirement, to qualify for the renovation plan. I see my colleague for Quebec East (Mr. Duquet) and 1 am sure that people in Quebec East will be taking advantage of this program. In fact, they have already started to do so, and now more people will be able to benefit as a result of the additional funds that have been allocated. Another important aspect that was well received and which has not been given much attention by the official opposition is the last program I am going to discuss. There is also the Canada Mortgage Renewal Plan. It has been extended from November 12, 1982 to December 31
1983.	And there is a provision under which homeowners who must allocate more than 30 per cent of their gross income to mortgage payments will be eligible, after June 28, for a nontaxable cash grant of up to $3,000. The significant aspect is that interest deferment will no longer be required before someone becomes eligible for a grant.
Those are the programs announced in the budget which have been acclaimed by contractors, construction workers and realtors who represent a sector of economic activity which is vitally important in my riding and in my province. After those announcements by the Minister of Finance, a good many people were so enthusiastic that they made a series of phone calls in the ridings of Quebec-in mine, certainly-to let my colleagues know how pleased they were about this new housing policy.
I also read a few Toronto area newspaper articles stating just how relieved the construction industry was about this. 1 think it was in The Toronto Sun, and there was also an article along the same lines in The Globe and Mail. During the few minutes I have left, Mr. Speaker, I would like to mention the job creation budgets of the Department of Employment and Immigration. One thing I find very important in that department is the Canada community development Program. Over a period of two years, $300 million will be earmarked for community development projects and other direct job-creation programs. Community development projects create employment through local organizations which are responsible for
July 7, 1982

launching and supervising the projects. It is a major undertaking which has been a source of employment for many Canadians. Quite true, such projects or programs provide work for periods lasting ten, 15, 20 or 25 weeks, but a lot of people who joined those programs were able to gain experience and then join the regular labour force. Still in the same vein, it has been said that $150 million will be spent on construction activities related to federal projects including, among other things, marinas and regional airports.
While 1 am on the subject of marinas, I might mention that not long ago I attended the opening ceremonies of a marina in Lotbiniere which had been built partly under a community development program and partly with the assistance of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, with grants of $25,000 and $30,000 respectively. The people who worked on that project were very proud of their achievement on opening day, because they had played a part in the tourism development of the municipality of Lotbiniere and were able to acquire skills in a specific field. Since the work was done in a shop, they gained good experience and with their new skills they were able to offer their services in other fields. My riding was allotted $680,000 last year under the community development program, and I did not hear any negative remarks. On the contrary, I heard nothing but praise about that program and all the people in my riding expressed the hope that such programs would be maintained so that they could undertake new projects which could hardly be launched if it were not for those programs.
Quite a number of municipalities are seeking financial assistance to develop tourism and similar projects, and one of the very important programs of the Canadian government is the community development program. I want, therefore, to congratulate the Minister of Finance for allowing his colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to allocate additional funds to these job-creation programs. I should like to return briefly to the housing programs; because I dealt with the housing industry, I must also mention other categories of people who will benefit, namely the dealers who sell lumber, hardware, iron, wrought iron and-I have in mind some people who play a very important role in my constituency of Lotbiniere and the Bois-Franc region-furniture makers. As 1 said a while ago, if the construction industry is indeed at a standstill, there are some industries which may be worse off financially and employ-mentwise. So, if the building industry gets going again, it being the wheel 1 mentioned earlier, furniture manufacturers will sell their products to furniture stores, who will sell them to young couples buying homes. This means that three or four more building related industries will take on a new lease of life. 1 am sure those people too will welcome the impact of the housing programs.
Much has been done for small businesses. My colleague, the hon. member for Charlevoix and Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) had the opportunity
The Budget-Mr. Shields
this afternoon to deal with his Department programs: $400 million will be made available to small-business men, farmers and fishermen; interest rates will be reduced for them and also-I shall close on that point-quite a few people made representations to their MPs concerning the plight of farmers. Well, in his budget, the Minister of Finance, as stated more specifically on page 25 of the budget papers, declared that additional amounts of money, namely $100 million would be allocated over the next two years, in addition to which farmers in dire straits will be able to avail themselves of loans totalling $200 million, under the program. There again a 4 per cent interest rate rebate is available. It will also be possible for farmers to obtain Small Business Bond financing.
There then, Mr. Speaker, you have some of the components of the budget 1 wanted to mention; when I heard the motion of the opposition about the situation of pensioners, and family allowances, and after hearing allegations made previously which would have people believe that money will be saved on the backs of pensioners and mothers, the main point I wanted to make is this: adjustments have been made and benefits will result despite the fact that some pensioners on the basic pension rate may have to pay the Government of Canada taxes which will help the Canadian people as a whole through job creation: to my mind, that is important, Mr. Speaker.
