subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in this budget debate today. I wonder whether some hon. members, possibly the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), the hon. member for Scarborough Centre (Mr. Kelly) or the minister from Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador (Mr. Rompkey), could tell me how they could

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Shields
support a budget brought into this House which claims it is going to attack inflation and justify a $20 billion deficit. How in God's name is that going to fight inflation? That $20 billion deficit contributes to inflation. That one single item should point out to members of this House the idiocy of the budget and what it is doing. In seven months, November to June, the deficit has doubled. This is not only contributing to inflation but is eroding the savings of people and causing a loss of jobs.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) did not know what he was doing with his November budget. It stifled investment in this country from coast to coast. He said he was going to plug some loopholes and soak the rich, but the rich got away scot-free. The minister aimed for the rich but hit the middle-income families, the mainstay in our society. It is they who were hit with his November budget. The minister stifled investment across this country, absolutely killing the resource industry and the oil industry in the western provinces, causing the loss of a great many jobs.
What are the problems facing Canada today? Basically there are three; unemployment, high interest rates and inflation.
Let me deal first with unemployment. People across this country are frightened. They are frightened that they will lose their jobs and not be able to get another. They are frightened about what would happen if their unemployment insurance ran out. Would they have to go on welfare? Let me deal with some of the problems in my area of northeastern Alberta. Unemployment there is at an all-time high. Certainly there is a recession in the world, but of all countries, Canada was better equipped to face a downturn in the economy than any other country in the western world.
What did the June 28 budget do for the millions of Canadians affected as a result of high unemployment? In one part of the budget it was indicated that $800 million, close to a billion dollars, will be spent on make-work projects. However, when you really go through the document and begin to analyse it, you see that the total amount earmarked for job creation in Canada is about $150 million. Talk about misrepresentation!
Go with me for a moment to the pre-National Energy Program days and the first budget. Go with me for a moment to the second budget of last November. Let us remember what the climate of the economy was then. Let us remember the investment that was waiting to develop the oil sands in northeastern Alberta. Let us remember that Imperial Oil was ready to go ahead with the Cold Lake project, a direct capital investment of some $13 billion creating right across this country, from coast to coast, in virtually every province, 200,000 jobs.
Do you remember the Alsands consortium at the point they were two years ago before this government came to power, ready to invest $13 billion and create jobs virtually in every province from coast to coast? That project was right in the very heart of my riding. It did not affect only northeastern Alberta and the Athabasca riding; it would affect the riding of the member for Lincoln. It would also affect the riding of the
member from Scarborough Centre. Both he and the member from Lincoln recognize this fully.
Instead, what happened was a disaster. We hear excuses from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), consistently saying: "We were ready to go ahead and we still are; they could go ahead but it is not economically viable any more." He compares these two megaprojects in northern Alberta with the one in the Colorado oil shales that Exxon decided not to go ahead with in the United States. He always fails to point out that in the Exxon project and the Colorado oil shales, the recovery cost per barrel of oil in that project was in the neighbourhood of $80 to $85 per barrel. It was a form of hard rock mining. The oil was in shale, and they do not know how to handle it yet. The technology is in place today to produce oil by the in situ process in the Cold Lake area and by the mining process in northeastern Alberta at Fort McMurray, the Alsands project. The technology is in place to produce it at close to world price.
I agree that there is not much margin for error. I agree that there is a possibility that world oil prices could drop, causing some hardship. But think for a moment of what is happening today. We are importing energy at world prices, paying in American dollars what we must buy on the foreign exchange with Canadian dollars. We are buying 400,000 barrels of oil per day from Mexico, from Saudi Arabia, from Venezuela, using American funds for which we must exchange Canadian funds. That means putting pressure on our Canadian dollar, an outflow of capital.
What would have happened, and what could happen if this government came to its senses, is that it could have gone to Germany and Japan and said: "Gentlemen, we know that you people are starving for oil. We know that over in Germany security of supply is the main and paramount thing you want for the next century or for the next two or three decades. We invite you to invest in a massive project to develop the oil sands, because locked in those oil sands is an amount of reserves every bit as much as now exists in the Middle East in the Arab countries." Hon. members may not know this, but the total reserves in the Athabasca, Alberta oil sands exceed the reserves that are presently in the Middle East. I am talking about known reserves.
To me, Germany would be happy to invest, Japan would be happy to invest, the United States would be happy to invest, if we said to them: "Help us develop, help us produce from these oil sands; and when we reach oil self-sufficiency, we will sell you the surplus." We would be protecting ourselves at the same time as we would be helping ourselves and helping those countries in the western world.
There is a precedent for this. Why do you think, Mr. Speaker, that Japan went in with Dome Petroleum and loaned them money for development in the Beaufort Sea? Do you not think that Japan recognized an opportunity where we might find in the Beaufort developments or in the offshore enough oil for our needs and that we may then sell to them? Do you not think that the Japanese government did not realize at that point in
July 7, 1982

time-we can go back three years now-that Canada is a country they can have a secure supply of energy from? Those countries that do not have the necessary oil to keep their economy rolling would be happy to invest in this country? But not under the present national energy policy as it was implemented. That is because this Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, when he introduced through the Minister of Finance the first budget that became the national energy policy told the world that we are thieves in this country. He said, in effect: "We will enter into a deal with you, but believe me, we will steal from you down the way because we are going to change the rules." That is outright theft of assets of foreign investors. My head hangs in shame when 1 think of it.
Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that we would not have the megaprojects going and employment at an all-time high, that we would be looking right across this country, that we would be looking to other parts of the world for skilled labour? We would be saying that we need so many welders, that we need technical people. We would be encouraging our young people to go to universities and to technical schools. Instead, what is happening now is that those young people are telephoning my office, as 1 am sure they are phoning the offices of other members, and are asking where are the jobs that this government promised to them. They ask: "Where are the jobs for which I enrolled in university four or five years ago?" They ask: "Where are the jobs in the oil industry that I was promised when I enrolled in petroleum engineering?" They ask: "Where are the jobs in accounting that I was promised when I enrolled in commerce?" Indeed, they ask: "Where are the jobs for teachers; I was told they would be needing teachers in 1982?" And then they ask: "Indeed, where can I get a job- period-nothing else, I just want a job. I went to university for three or four years", or "I went to technical school", or "I am graduating from high school and I cannot get a job." That is what we are doing to our country. That is what we are going to continue to do to our country as long as we allow this Liberal government with its present policies to exist in Canada.
I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I was home on the weekend at Fort McMurray. I received a call from a gentleman 1 have known for ten years. This man is a qualified tradesman. He said he had an emergency and would like to talk with me. I am telling this House now something I hope all members will listen to, including the member from Scarborough Centre. I want them to think about this for a minute. I went to his home. His wife and family disappeared into the bedroom because he wanted to talk to me privately. He said: "Mr. Shields, Jack, I have a problem; I have no money and 1 have no food in the house, and we have not had anything since lunch." The children ate the last of the cereal. He took me to his fridge; there was nothing in it. He had run out of unemployment insurance and he was too damned proud to walk down to the social development agency and ask for welfare. That is what we are facing in this country and it is getting
The Budget-Mr. Shields
worse. I hear one of those cheeky members opposite saying "We told you."
Mr. Speaker, in the pre-national energy policy days investment was begging to come into this country to develop some of our resources. We should not be importing 400,000 barrels of oil a day at a cost which is loaded on that very taxpayer who cannot feed his family and himself and who must now go on welfare. When that man was employed he was paying taxes and we were importing oil from offshore. Is that reasonable and intelligent? I do not think it is and I do not think that most Canadians think so either.
I have spoken to lawyers in my riding who tell me that in 10 or 15 years of practice they have never experienced a year with more divorce applications. A milestone was reached last month in Fort McMurray when there were more divorce actions before the courts than in any prior month. One reason for this was desertion, because men could not bear to go home day after day and tell their wives they could not get a job. Put yourself in the place of the man who cannot feed his children or that man who saw his children eat the last of the food that was in the house and was too proud to go on welfare or call a neighbour and say he was broke. That is the sort of situation people are facing. As a result, many men just leave because they cannot face their wives and family day after day.
Unemployment is not just a figure that shows 1.5 million or two million people out of work. It means the breakup of families, desertion and in some cases suicide, wife beating and child abuse. Funny things happen to people when they lose their self-respect and that is what is taking place today.
The government can do something about all this, Mr. Speaker. Instead of introducing massive job-training programs it could enter into long-term deals with countries like Japan and Germany. It would be simple and straightforward and those countries would develop our resources and create jobs. They would invest their money if they were guaranteed security of supply. We need only consider what is happening with that gas line that is going into Europe from Siberia. Some of the member NATO countries are telling Germany and France not to buy gas from Siberia as that will make them subject to the economic whims of Russia.
There is gas everywhere in this country, Mr. Speaker. It is a saleable commodity that we should develop. We should encourage investment from offshore because we do not have the money to invest in the tar sands megaprojects ourselves. We must rely on outside capital and we all know that. It is just common sense. We should go ahead with these projects and contribute to the security supply of our NATO allies and various friendly trading nations like Japan. Instead, we find that Japan is going to ship us ten more cars this month than last month. Of course, the government realizes that does not look good politically so the entry of the cars is delayed. At the same time, however, the Russian Lada, which sells here for $6,000, is being dumped on our market. The whole situation is

July 7, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Shields
crazy, Mr. Speaker, and I have to sit here and listen to hon. members opposite attempt to justify this so-called budget.
We still depend on the Middle East for security of supply of oil. Our purchases from that area are draining our dollar reserve because we must buy U.S. dollars to pay for it. That puts pressure on the Canadian dollar and so, in order to attract more dollars, interest rates must be raised. With just one megaproject, interest rates would drop by at least 2 per cent. It would be a signal to the world that we realize we made a mistake and that we intend to get the oil industry back on stream to lead us out of this economic mess.
We want and need foreign investment in this country, Mr. Speaker, but the government does not seem to realize that. It is concerned with getting after the civil servants and nailing them with a 6 per cent increase. It will become known as the 6 per cent government. It was going to wrestle inflation to the ground two years ago but now it will wrestle it to 6 per cent.
What can be done about high interest rates, Mr. Speaker? The deficit can be reduced. If the government was responsible to an annual meeting of shareholders it would be doing something about that today. The Minister of Finance brought in a budget in November and seven months later he admits he was 100 per cent wrong. Having said there would be a $10 billion deficit, he now says it will be a $20 billion deficit. He may be a nice man, kind with admirable qualities, but he should not be allowed to remain in the job. He made the fundamental error of forecasting a deficit that was 100 per cent wrong. In any other line of business he would lose his job.
How can the deficit be reduced? One way would be for the government to admit that it does not need a $150 million or $200 million budget to run advertising programs in all its departments. We are going to cut back to $50 million at a direct saving to the taxpayer of $100 million. I say that you do not commit to capital projects when you do not have the money. You do not build a new embassy in Washington when the facilities that our embassy staff now occupy will do them for two, three, four years, or however long it takes until we have the money and can afford to build. When I questioned the Prime Minister about whether he would cut back in those areas, he said, "Well, I am sure the hon. member could find lots of areas to cut back, lots of building projects." What building projects do we want to cut back? I say, Mr. Speaker, that every project on the books right now which is not deemed an emergency should be stopped.
We talk about irresponsible corporations and so on. I am sure all hon. members read the paper, but let me point out what happens to Imperial Oil when they feel the pinch. They have shareholders that they have to report to, so what are they doing? They are laying off and cutting back their staff by 500 people. They have curtailed all capital expenditure and are retiring the president of their company three years early. I am
sure that many hon. members would agree with me that it is too bad we could not retire the present leader of this great corporation of Canada three years early. However, maybe if they think hard enough, work hard enough at it and listen to what their constituents are telling them, they just may find enough courage to do it.
I want to turn for a moment to the leader of the NDP, Mr. Speaker. 1 listened with real attention to his remarks on the first day of the budget debate. He said we do not want less government, we want more government. That was his message. We want lower taxes, lower interest rates but more government. How in God's name do you pay for more government without taxes or higher interest rates? You cannot, it is ridiculous, but again that is the NDP. We hear the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) repeatedly saying that government should get more involved, that it should go out and buy not little oil companies but big ones. What is the matter with Imperial? He fails to recognize that if the government does not have the money to do it, the taxpayer is going to be whipped again to pay for these astronomical bills and debts which the NDP would build up. That is totally and absolutely irresponsible.
In closing, Madam Speaker, I would just like to say that the biggest problem facing our country is unemployment, which problem could be addressed very quickly if we were to encourage investment from offshore. As I said, Germany and Japan, countries which do not have an oil supply, could come in and start developing the oil sands where there are massive reserves on the condition that, once we reach self-sufficiency here in Canada, we will then sell them the surplus. We will have lots of takers because in five years it is going to be security of supply once again that is most important. We will have those takers, and once that happens, Madam Speaker, we will have jobs right across the country. We are a sparsely populated country and we could be selling some of the abundance of reserves we have in oil, coal and minerals to countries that do not have them but who do want security of supply.
